title: Part II: Accounts from Incomplete Records

learn.hook: The paan shop near your school probably keeps a notebook of cash and a list of who owes money, and nothing else. That is accounting from incomplete records.
points: Incomplete records (often called the single entry system) are accounting records not kept strictly on the double entry system.
Usually only a cash book and personal accounts of debtors and creditors are kept; real accounts (assets) and nominal accounts (expenses, incomes) are generally not kept.
Features: no uniformity (methods differ from firm to firm); business and personal transactions are often mixed; heavy reliance on vouchers, memory and information from outside sources.
It is suited to small sole traders and partnership firms; companies cannot use it, because the law requires double entry books.

example.q: A small florist keeps a cash diary and a list of hotel customers who pay monthly. She does not record rent, wages or her shop fittings in any account. What kind of records are these?
steps: Only cash and personal (debtors) accounts are kept.
Nominal accounts (rent, wages) and real accounts (fittings) are missing.
So these are incomplete records, not a double entry system.

learn.reallife: Many street vendors registered under PM SVANidhi keep only cash and dues records; as they grow, digital apps help them shift to complete books.

topics.title: Reasons for incomplete records and their limitations

learn.hook: Incomplete records are cheap and easy, like cooking without a recipe. But when the tax officer or the bank manager asks for proof, the shortcut becomes expensive.
points: Reasons: used by small traders with few transactions; owners lack accounting knowledge; low cost (no trained accountant needed); simple and less time-consuming.

Limitations: no trial balance, so arithmetical accuracy cannot be checked; true profit or loss is hard to find; a proper balance sheet cannot be prepared; not acceptable to tax authorities as complete books; banks hesitate to lend; frauds and errors are hard to detect; no control over assets.
Profit can still be estimated by comparing capital at two dates (the statement of affairs method).
The conversion method (rebuilding full double entry final accounts from incomplete records) is outside the CBSE Class 11 syllabus; only the statement of affairs method is studied.

example.q: A trader with incomplete records applies for a loan. Give two reasons the bank may hesitate.
steps: Without double entry books, his profit figure cannot be verified.
He cannot produce a reliable balance sheet showing assets and liabilities.
So the bank cannot judge his repaying capacity or the security.
example.answer: Profit cannot be verified and no reliable balance sheet exists.

learn.reallife: GST registration nudges many small Indian businesses to keep fuller records, because input tax credit needs proper invoices and books.

topics.title: Statement of affairs and finding capital

learn.hook: If you can't trace every transaction, take two photographs instead: one at the start of the year and one at the end. Each photograph of assets and liabilities is a statement of affairs.
points: A statement of affairs is a statement of all assets and liabilities on a date, prepared from incomplete records. The difference is the capital: Capital = Total assets − Total liabilities.
Format: like a balance sheet, liabilities and capital on the left, assets on the right; capital is the balancing figure.

Statement of affairs vs balance sheet: the statement of affairs is prepared from incomplete records and values are often estimates; capital is a balancing figure; omissions are hard to detect. A balance sheet is prepared from a double entry ledger, values come from ledger balances, and capital is taken from the capital account.
Opening statement of affairs gives opening capital; closing statement of affairs gives closing capital.

example.q: On 1 April: cash ₹15,000, stock ₹60,000, debtors ₹45,000, furniture ₹30,000, creditors ₹40,000. On 31 March: cash ₹20,000, stock ₹75,000, debtors ₹55,000, furniture ₹27,000, creditors ₹47,000. Find opening and closing capital.

learn.reallife: Income tax officers in India sometimes estimate a small trader's income by comparing his net worth at two dates, the same idea as a statement of affairs.

learn.hook: If your piggy bank grew from ₹1,000 to ₹1,500, did you earn ₹500? Only if you didn't take money out or put extra in. Business profit works the same way.
points: Profit = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Opening capital.
Drawings are added back because they reduced closing capital but were not a loss of the business.
Additional capital is deducted because it increased closing capital but was not earned.
A negative result means a loss.

The formula can be rearranged to find any missing figure: Opening capital = Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital − Profit; Drawings = Profit + Opening capital + Additional capital − Closing capital.

example.q: Opening capital ₹2,00,000; closing capital ₹2,60,000; drawings ₹30,000; additional capital ₹40,000. Find profit.
steps: Closing capital + drawings = 2,60,000 + 30,000 = ₹2,90,000.
Less additional capital: 2,90,000 − 40,000 = ₹2,50,000 (adjusted closing capital).
Less opening capital: 2,50,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹50,000 profit.

learn.reallife: A Kolkata sari trader who doesn't keep full books can still tell her CA how much her business earned by listing what she owned and owed at both year-ends, plus what she took home.

topics.title: Statement of profit or loss with adjustments

learn.hook: The capital-comparison profit is a rough figure. Before reporting it, an accountant charges interest on capital, adds interest on drawings and accounts for items like depreciation that the closing figures may have missed.
points: Statement of profit or loss format: Closing capital + Drawings − Additional capital = Adjusted closing capital; less Opening capital = Profit before adjustments.

Then: Less interest on capital; add interest on drawings. Also adjust for depreciation, provision for doubtful debts, further bad debts, outstanding expenses (less) and accrued income or prepaid expenses (add), if they have not already been reflected in the closing statement of affairs.
Interest on capital is usually calculated on opening capital (and on additional capital from its date).
The final figure is the net profit (or loss) for the year.
Best practice: apply asset-related adjustments (depreciation, bad debts, provisions, outstanding items) while preparing the closing statement of affairs, so that closing capital is correct.

example.q: Profit before adjustments ₹60,000. Opening capital ₹2,00,000; interest on capital 5%. Interest on drawings ₹1,000. Find net profit.
steps: Interest on capital = 5% × 2,00,000 = ₹10,000.
